title: Microplastics Detected in Blood of 84% of Severe Heart Attack Patients
excerpt: Italian researchers found micro- and nanoplastics in the coronary blood of the vast majority of patients who suffered serious heart attacks, with smokers six times more likely to carry plastic particles.
body:
• Micro- and nanoplastics were found in the coronary blood of 84% of patients who suffered severe heart attacks, compared with 40% of those with chronic heart disease and 32% with normal arteries.
  • Polyethylene, the world's most widely produced plastic, was the most common type detected and appeared in 97% of patients who tested positive.
  • Smokers were six times more likely to have microplastics in their blood; all patients who smoked and had higher air pollution exposure tested positive.
  • The study does not prove microplastics cause heart attacks, but adds to growing evidence linking plastic pollution to cardiovascular risk.

Plastic particles have been found in the coronary blood of 84% of patients who suffered the most severe form of heart attack, according to a study published in the European Heart Journal on July 14. The research marks the first time scientists have measured micro- and nanoplastic concentrations directly in the blood vessels supplying the heart.

Researchers at Sapienza University of Rome, the University of Verona, and the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli in Naples analyzed blood from 61 patients undergoing coronary angiography. The patients fell into three groups: those experiencing an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), the most dangerous type of heart attack; those with chronic ischemic heart disease; and those with normal coronary arteries.

Stark Differences Across Patient Groups

The results showed a clear gradient. Among STEMI patients, 84% had detectable micro- and nanoplastics in their coronary blood. That figure dropped to 40% among chronic heart disease patients and 32% among controls with normal arteries. Heart attack patients also carried a wider variety of plastic types in their blood.

Polyethylene — used in plastic bags, bottles, and packaging — was the dominant material, appearing in 97% of patients who tested positive. The findings build on a landmark 2024 study in the New England Journal of Medicine that found microplastics inside arterial plaques of surgery patients, who then faced 4.5 times the risk of heart attack, stroke, or death over the following three years.

"These findings do not prove that microplastics cause heart attacks, but they reveal a strong association between environmental exposures, microplastics in the blood and cardiovascular disease."

— Professor Emanuele Barbato, Sapienza University of Rome

Smoking and Air Pollution Amplify the Risk

The study found smoking was one of the strongest predictors of microplastic contamination. Smokers were six times more likely than nonsmokers to have plastic particles in their blood. Air pollution told a similar story — patients exposed to higher long-term levels of PM2.5 particulate matter were significantly more likely to carry microplastics.

The overlap was striking: every patient who both smoked and lived with elevated air pollution tested positive for plastic particles. Among people who neither smoked nor experienced higher pollution, the detection rate fell to just 12.5%.

"Smoking might make it easier for micro and nanoplastics to enter the bloodstream via the lungs. Air pollution may act in a similar way," said Barbato, who directs the Cardiology Unit at Sant'Andrea University Hospital in Rome.

The Inflammation Connection

Heart attack patients in the study also showed elevated levels of inflammatory molecules, including tumor necrosis factor-α and interleukin-6. These markers point to systemic inflammation — a mechanism researchers believe could explain how plastic particles contribute to cardiovascular damage.

An accompanying editorial by Professor Andreas Daiber of the Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, placed the findings in a broader context. "Experimental studies indicate that they trigger key mechanisms of vascular injury, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction," Daiber and colleagues wrote.

"Plastic pollution may represent a previously underestimated cardiovascular risk factor. Addressing this challenge will require coordinated efforts across disciplines and policy domains."

— Professor Andreas Daiber, Johannes Gutenberg University

A Growing Body of Evidence

The study's first author, Dr. Pasquale Paolisso, noted that microplastics have already been detected in human blood, lungs, placenta, and breast milk. "Very little was known about whether these particles are present in the coronary circulation," he said.

The research has limitations. The sample size of 61 patients is small, and the study cannot establish causation. Researchers did not control for all possible confounding factors, such as socioeconomic status or diet. Still, the consistency with prior findings — particularly the 2024 NEJM study linking plastics in arterial plaques to worse outcomes — strengthens the case for further investigation.

What Comes Next

The researchers called for policies targeting air pollution, tobacco exposure, and environmental plastic contamination. Larger studies are now needed to determine whether reducing plastic exposure can meaningfully lower cardiovascular risk. For now, the study adds microplastics to a growing list of environmental factors that cardiologists must consider alongside cholesterol, blood pressure, and smoking when assessing heart disease risk.
